card.summary_ko: 병자호란 끝에 인조가 남한산성을 나와 삼전도에서 청 태종 앞에 삼배구고두례를 올리고 항복한 1637년 1월 30일의 기록입니다. 이조참판 정온의 상소와, 항복 의식·하사품·피로인들의 통곡까지 《인조실록》이 전합니다.
card.summary_en: The Veritable Records entry for the 30th day of the first month of 1637, when, at the end of the Manchu invasion of 1636, King Injo left Namhansanseong and submitted to the Qing ruler at Samjeondo with the rite of three kneelings and nine head-knockings. It includes Jeong On's protest memorial, the ceremony, the gifts and the wailing of the captives.

notes.ko:
**저자** 《인조실록》은 개인의 저작이 아니라 국가가 임명한 실록청이 사관의 기록(사초)과 관청 문서를 모아 편찬한 공식 기록입니다. 표준적인 설명에 따르면 인조 때의 기록은 효종 대에 편찬되어 1653년에 완성되었습니다. 당시 조정은 인조반정(1623)을 이끈 서인 계열이 주도하고 있었고, 그런 만큼 서술에는 편찬 시기의 정치적 입장이 스며 있을 수 있다고 이해됩니다. 실록은 국왕도 열람할 수 없는 것이 원칙이었으나, 편찬 주체는 곧 당대의 집권 세력입니다.

**시대적 맥락** 1636년 청(淸)이 국호를 정하고 황제를 칭한 뒤 조선에 군신 관계를 요구하자 조선 조정은 둘로 갈렸습니다. 김상헌 등 척화파는 명에 대한 의리와 오랑캐와는 화친할 수 없다는 명분을 앞세웠고, 최명길 등 주화파는 국가와 백성의 보존을 위해 현실적으로 협상해야 한다고 주장했습니다. 병자호란이 일어나 인조는 남한산성에서 약 45일을 버텼으나 강화도가 함락되고 식량이 떨어져 항복했습니다. 이 기사에서 정온이 최명길을 지목해 비판하는 것은 이 대립을 보여 줍니다. 이후 소현세자·봉림대군과 많은 백성이 청으로 끌려갔고, 조선은 명과의 관계를 끊고 청에 신속했습니다.

**배경** 이 판은 중국어 위키문헌의 전사본이며, 한 달의 기사 가운데 1637년(인조 15) 1월 30일 항목을 발췌했습니다. 11월 30일의 청 사신 환송 기사는 삼전도와 무관하여 뺐습니다. 청 황제를 이 글은 '한(汗)'이라 부르고, 인조 자신은 '황제'라고 말합니다.

**의의** 조선 사대부가 가장 치욕으로 여긴 사건의 공식 기록입니다. 삼배구고두례, 하사품을 받아 입는 장면, 끌려가는 이들의 통곡이 건조한 실록 문체로 기록되어 있어 사료로서 가치가 큽니다.

**형식과 주제** 편년체 실록이며 문장은 사실 위주의 한문입니다. 정온의 상소는 척화파의 논리를, 나머지는 의식의 절차를 보여 줍니다. 주제는 국가의 항복과 신하의 의리, 굴욕 속의 국왕입니다.

**읽기 도움**
- 出降(출항): 성을 나와 항복함.
- 三拜九叩頭禮(삼배구고두례): 세 번 무릎 꿇고 아홉 번 머리를 조아리는 청의 신하 예법.
- 嬪宮(빈궁): 세자빈. 大君(대군): 왕의 아들(여기서는 봉림·인평대군).
- 班荊(반형): 풀을 깔고 앉음.
- 國寶(국보): 임금의 도장. 誥命(고명)·玉冊(옥책): 명이 내린 책봉 문서.
- 龍胡(용호)·龍骨大(용골대): 청 장수 용골대(잉굴다이)로 이해됩니다.
- 迎逢者(영봉자)와 金石乙屎(김석을시)는 의미나 인물이 분명치 않아 잠정적으로 옮겼습니다.
notes.en:
**About the author** The Veritable Records of King Injo (Injo sillok) is not an individual's work but an official record compiled by a state-appointed bureau from historians' drafts and government documents. By the standard account the records of Injo's reign were compiled under King Hyojong and completed in 1653. The court of that time was led by the Westerners (Seoin), the faction that had carried out the Injo Restoration of 1623, so the narrative can be read as bearing the political stance of its compilers. By principle even the king could not read the Records, but the compilers were in practice the ruling party of the day.

**Historical context** In 1636 the Qing proclaimed their dynasty and the emperor's title and demanded a ruler-subject relationship from Joseon, which split the court. The anti-peace faction (*cheokhwa*), such as Kim Sang-heon, stood on loyalty to the Ming and the principle that there could be no accommodation with barbarians; the pro-peace faction (*juhwa*), such as Choe Myeong-gil, argued that negotiation was necessary to preserve the state and its people. After the Manchu invasion began, Injo held out at Namhansanseong for about 45 days, but Ganghwa fell and provisions ran out, and he surrendered. Jeong On's attack on Choe Myeong-gil in this entry shows that division. Afterwards Crown Prince Sohyeon, Prince Bongnim and many commoners were taken to the Qing, and Joseon broke with the Ming and became the Qing's tributary.

**Background** This is the Chinese Wikisource transcription; the excerpt is the entry for the 30th day of the first month of 1637 (Injo 15). The 30th-day entry of the eleventh month, on seeing off a Qing envoy, is omitted as unrelated to Samjeondo. The text calls the Qing ruler *han* (khan), while Injo himself calls him "emperor."

**Significance** It is the official record of the event Joseon scholar-officials regarded as their deepest humiliation. The three kneelings and nine head-knockings, the scene of receiving and wearing gifts, and the wailing of those led away are set down in the dry style of the Records, giving it great value as a source.

**Form and themes** An annalistic record in factual hanmun. Jeong On's memorial presents the logic of the anti-peace camp; the rest sets out the steps of the ceremony. Its themes are a state's surrender and a subject's duty, and a king in humiliation.

**Reading help**
- 出降 (chulhang): to come out and surrender.
- 三拜九叩頭禮 (sambae gugodu rye): three kneelings and nine head-knockings, the Qing court's rite for subjects.
- 嬪宮 (bingung): the Crown Princess; 大君 (daegun): a king's son (here Princes Bongnim and Inpyeong).
- 班荊 (banhyeong): to sit on spread brush.
- 國寶 (gukbo): the royal seal; 誥命 (gomyeong), 玉冊 (okchaek): Ming investiture documents.
- 龍胡 (Yongho), 龍骨大 (Yonggoldae): understood as the Qing general Inggūldai.
- 迎逢者 and 金石乙屎 have unclear meaning or identity and are translated tentatively.

paragraphs.en: ## The 30th Day of the First Month (Injo 15, 1637)

paragraphs.orig: ○庚午，吏曹參判鄭蘊上箚曰：臣之自決，正爲不忍見殿下今日之事，而一縷殘命，三日猶在，臣實怪之。鳴吉旣使殿下，稱臣出降，君臣之分已定矣。臣之於君，不但以承順爲恭，可爭則爭之可也。彼若求納皇朝之印，則殿下當爭之曰：「自祖宗受用此印，今將三百年。此印還納於明朝，不可納於淸國」云；彼若求助攻天朝之兵，殿下當爭之曰：「天朝父子之恩，淸國亦知之。敎子攻父，有關倫紀。非但攻之者有罪，敎之者亦不可」云，則彼雖凶狡，亦必諒矣。伏願殿下，以此二者爭之，無得罪於天下後世，不勝幸甚。臣命在垂盡，旣不能扈駕，又不能哭辭於路左，臣罪大矣。請遞臣職，使得瞑目。○龍、馬兩胡，來城外，趣上出城。上着藍染衣，乘白馬，盡去儀仗，率侍從五十餘人，由西門出城，王世子從焉。百官落後者，立於西門內，搥胸哭踊。上下山，班荊而坐。俄而，淸兵被甲者數百騎馳來。上曰：「此何爲者耶？」都承旨李景稷對曰：「此似我國之所謂迎逢者也。」良久，龍胡等至。上離坐迎之，行再揖禮，分東西而坐。龍胡等致慰，上答曰：「今日之事，專恃皇帝之言與兩大人之宣力矣。」龍胡曰：「今而後，兩國爲一家，有何憂哉？日已晩矣，請速去。」遂馳馬前導。上只率三公及判書、承旨各五人，翰、注各一人，世子率侍講院、翊衛司諸官，隨詣三田渡。望見，汗張黃屋而坐，甲冑而帶弓劍者，爲方陣而擁立左右，張樂鼓吹，略倣華制。上步至陣前，龍胡等留上於陣門東。龍胡入報，出傳汗言曰：「前日之事，欲言則長矣。今能勇決而來，深用喜幸。」上答曰：「天恩罔極。」龍胡等引入，設席於壇下北面，請上就席，使淸人臚唱。上行三拜九叩頭禮。龍胡等引上由陣東門出，更由東北隅而入，使坐於壇東。大君以下，自江都被執而來，列立於壇下少西矣。龍胡以汗言，請上登壇，汗南面而坐，上坐於東北隅西面，而淸王子三人，以次連坐，王世子又坐其下，竝西面。又淸王子四人，坐於西北隅東面，二大君連坐於其下。我國侍臣，給席於壇下東隅，江都被執諸臣，入坐於壇下西隅，進茶一杯，汗使龍骨大，告我諸侍臣曰：「今則兩國爲一家矣。欲觀射藝，其各效技。」從官等答曰：「來此者皆文官，故不能射矣。」龍胡强之，遂令衛率鄭以重出射，而弓矢與本國之制不同，五射而俱不中。淸王子及諸將，雜沓竝射以爲戲。俄令進饌、行酒，酒三行，命撤杯盤。將撤，有從胡二人，各牽狗而至于汗前，汗親自割肉投之。上辭出，嬪宮以下士大夫家屬之被執者，皆聚於一處。龍胡以汗言，請嬪宮、大君夫人出拜，觀者灑泣，其實代以內人云。龍胡等以汗所贈白馬，具玲瓏鞍牽來，上親執轡，從臣受之。龍胡等又將貂裘而來，傳汗言曰：「此物，當初意欲相贈而持來。今見本國衣制不同，非敢强使着之也，只表情意而已。」上受而着之，入庭展謝，使都承旨李景稷，奉國寶以進，龍胡受之而去。俄而，來詰曰：「誥命、玉冊，何以不納耶？」上曰：「玉冊則曾於甲子年，因變亂失之。誥命則送于江華，兵戈顚倒之時，難保其獲全，而如或有之，則追納何難？」龍胡唯唯而去。又以貂裘三領，招三公着之；五領，招五卿着之；五領，招五承旨着之，謂之曰：「奉主上，勤勞於山城，故以此爲贈耳。」受賜者皆伏謝於庭。洪瑞鳳、張維入伏於庭，請得尋見老母，金石乙屎怒叱之。上地坐田中，待其進退，日晡後，始令還都。王世子及嬪宮曁二大君及夫人，竝令留置，蓋將以北行故也。上退，入見嬪宮於幕次，留崔鳴吉，姑令陪衛焉。上由所波津，乘船而渡。時，津卒死亡殆盡，只有空船二艘，百官爭渡，至攀御衣而上船。上旣渡，汗隨後馳來，由淺灘渡軍，就桑田箚陣，令龍胡率護行軍兵，挾路左右，導上而行。被擄子女望見，號哭皆曰：「吾君、吾君，捨我而去乎？」挾路啼號者，以萬數。人定時，始達京城，御昌慶宮養和堂。
paragraphs.en:
○ On the gyeongo day, Jeong On, Vice Minister of Personnel, submitted a memorial: "That I took my own life was precisely because I could not bear to see what has become of Your Majesty today; yet a thread of remaining life has lasted three days, and I truly wonder at it. Myeong-gil has already made Your Majesty declare yourself a subject and come out to surrender; the division between ruler and subject is already settled. In my relation to my lord, it is not only obedience that is reverence; where one can remonstrate, to remonstrate is right. If they ask to have the seal of the imperial dynasty handed over, Your Majesty should contend: 'Since our ancestors received and used this seal, it will soon be three hundred years. This seal may be returned to the Ming; it cannot be handed over to the Qing.' If they ask for troops to help attack the Heavenly Court, Your Majesty should contend: 'The Qing too know the father-and-son favour of the Heavenly Court. To teach a son to attack his father concerns the bonds of human relations. Not only is the one who attacks guilty; the one who teaches it is also in the wrong.' Then, though they are fierce and cunning, they will surely understand. I humbly beg Your Majesty to contend with them on these two points, so as to incur no guilt before the world and posterity; I would be unspeakably fortunate. My life is at its last; I could neither accompany the carriage nor weep in farewell by the roadside. My crime is great. I beg to be dismissed from my post, that I may close my eyes in peace."

○ The two barbarians, Ryong and Ma, came outside the city and urged the king to come out of it. The king wore blue-dyed clothes and rode a white horse; he dismissed all the ceremonial guards and went out by the west gate with more than fifty attendants, the Crown Prince following. Officials who lagged behind stood inside the west gate, beating their chests and weeping and leaping about. The king came down the hill and sat on spread brush. Presently several hundred armoured Qing horsemen came galloping up. The king said, "What are these?" The Chief Royal Secretary Yi Gyeong-jik answered, "These seem to be what in our country we call 'welcomers.'" After a long while, Ryong and his party arrived. The king left his seat to receive them and made a double bow, and they sat east and west of each other. Ryong and his party offered condolences, and the king answered: "In today's affair I rely solely on the Emperor's word and the exertions of the two great men." Ryong said: "From now on the two countries will be one family; what is there to worry about? The day is already late, please go quickly." Then they galloped ahead to lead the way. The king took with him only the three high ministers, five each of the board ministers and royal secretaries, and one each of the Hallim and the recorders; the Crown Prince took the officials of the Crown Prince's Tutorial Office and Guard; and they followed to Samjeondo. In view, the Khan had a yellow tent spread and was seated; armoured men with bows and swords stood in square formation on the left and right, with music and drums playing, roughly imitating the Chinese system. The king went on foot to the front of the formation, and Ryong and his party kept the king at the east of the formation gate. Ryong went in to report and came out relaying the Khan's words: "As for the previous matter, to speak of it would be long. That you have now come with resolute courage, I am deeply glad." The king answered: "Heaven's grace is boundless." Ryong and his party led him in, laid a mat before the altar facing north, asked the king to take his place on the mat, and had a Qing man call out the ceremony. The king performed the rite of three kneelings and nine head-knockings. Ryong and his party led the king out by the east gate of the formation, then in again by the northeast corner, and seated him at the east of the altar. The Grand Princes and others who had been seized at Ganghwa and brought here stood in a line a little west below the altar. Ryong, by the Khan's word, asked the king to ascend the altar; the Khan sat facing south, and the king sat at the northeast corner facing west, with three Qing princes seated in order beside him, and the Crown Prince seated below them, all facing west. Four more Qing princes sat at the northwest corner facing east, with the two Grand Princes seated in line below them. Our attendants were given mats at the east corner below the altar; the officials seized at Ganghwa entered and sat at the west corner below the altar. A cup of tea was offered. The Khan had Yonggolda tell our attendants: "Now the two countries are one family. We wish to watch some archery; each of you display your skill." The accompanying officials answered, "Those who have come here are all civil officials, so we cannot shoot." Ryong pressed them, and so the Guard Commander Jeong I-jung was ordered to shoot, but the bows and arrows differed from those of our country, and in five shots none hit. The Qing princes and generals mixed in and shot together as a game. Presently food was brought and wine passed; after three rounds of wine they ordered the cups and dishes cleared. As they were about to clear them, two barbarian attendants, each leading a dog, came before the Khan, and the Khan himself cut meat and threw it to them. The king asked leave and withdrew; the Crown Princess and the families of scholar-officials who had been seized were all gathered in one place. Ryong, by the Khan's word, asked the Crown Princess and the wives of the Grand Princes to come out and bow; the onlookers wept, but in fact, it is said, women of the inner court were substituted for them. Ryong and his party brought the white horse the Khan gave as a gift, with a gilded saddle, and the king himself took the reins and received it from his attendant. Ryong and his party also brought a sable coat, and said in the Khan's words: "This item I originally meant to give to you and so brought it; now I see that the clothing of your country differs, and I do not dare to force you to wear it. It only expresses my feeling." The king accepted it and put it on, entered the courtyard and made his thanks, and had the Chief Royal Secretary Yi Gyeong-jik present the state seal; Ryong received it and left. Presently he came back to press the matter: "The patent of investiture and the jade book, why are they not handed over?" The king said: "The jade book was lost in the Gapja year in the disturbance. The patent was sent to Ganghwa, and in the chaos of war it is hard to be sure it is intact; but if it exists, what difficulty is there in handing it over later?" Ryong assented and left. Then, with three sable coats, he summoned the three high ministers to put them on; with five, he summoned five board ministers to put them on; with five, he summoned five royal secretaries to put them on, and said to them: "Because you served your lord and toiled in the mountain fortress, I give you these." Those who received them all prostrated in thanks in the courtyard. Hong Seo-bong and Jang Yu went in and prostrated in the courtyard asking to be allowed to look for their old mothers, but Kim Seok-eulsi angrily scolded them. The king sat on the ground in a field to await their decision; after the afternoon, he was at last ordered to return to the capital. The Crown Prince, the Crown Princess, the two Grand Princes and their wives were all ordered to be kept behind, evidently because they were to be taken north. The king withdrew and went in to see the Crown Princess in the tent, and kept Choe Myeong-gil there for the moment to attend and guard her. The king crossed the river by boat at Sopa Ferry. At that time the ferrymen had almost all died, and there were only two empty boats; the officials fought to cross, even clutching the king's robes to climb aboard. After the king had crossed, the Khan galloped after him, took his army across by the shallows, camped at a mulberry field, and had Ryong lead the escort troops to line the road on both sides and guide the king along. The captured sons and daughters saw this and wailed, all saying, "Our lord, our lord, are you abandoning us and going?" Those lining the road weeping and crying out numbered in the tens of thousands. At the hour of curfew he finally reached the capital and lodged in Yanghwadang at Changgyeong Palace.
